part_title: Module 06 Visual Walkthrough — Application Architecture, Kinesis, Orders and Lambda

scenes.title: Module 06 — Build AI applications on AWS
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module Six. This opening slide is our map for building a complete AI application on AWS. Look at the six groups surrounding the glowing AI cloud. At the top left, Lambda runs application code and API Gateway exposes it to users. In the middle, Step Functions coordinates multi-step workflows, while AppConfig manages settings without changing the code. On the upper right, CodePipeline, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy help us build, test and release updates. The integration group on the lower left shows four different jobs: SQS buffers work, SNS sends notifications, EventBridge routes events and AppSync connects clients with application data. Amplify helps build and host the front end. Outposts and Wavelength extend selected workloads closer to on-premises systems or mobile users. Now follow the example path along the bottom, from left to right. A client submits a prompt through a web or mobile app. API Gateway receives the request and can invoke Lambda. Step Functions coordinates the required stages, using configuration supplied by AppConfig. A model performs the AI task, and the application returns its response. Notice that the model is only one part of the journey. The rest of these services make the AI feature accessible, manageable and reliable. We'll unpack them one diagram at a time.

scenes.title: Detect a transaction-rate spike
scenes.narration: This slide shows how an application detects an unusual burst of transactions. Start with the five numbered boxes across the top. Transactions arrive continuously and enter Kinesis Data Streams. A stream analysis component processes that incoming data and calculates the number of transactions per minute. When the calculated rate crosses a threshold, it triggers Lambda, which runs the notification logic and publishes through SNS. Now look at the graph in the bottom left. The orange dashed line is the threshold: two hundred transactions per minute. For most of the chart, the blue line remains below it. Then the rate rises to two hundred and forty per minute, crossing the threshold at the highlighted point. That's the event we want to respond to. The two panels on the right explain a subtle but important division of work. Continuous stream analysis keeps calculating the rate as new records arrive. Lambda does not do that continuous aggregation in this design; it responds when the threshold condition is met. It might create an alert message, include the observed rate, and send it using SNS to an operations team. Think of the stream analysis as the detector and Lambda as the responder. This separation lets the application monitor continuously without sending a notification for every individual transaction.

scenes.title: Process order history events
scenes.narration: Here we have a complete event-processing pipeline for an order history application. Follow the five steps across the top. First, the shopping application publishes an event when an order is placed. Second, Kinesis Data Streams receives the event. Third, Lambda processes a batch of events and transforms each one into an order record. Fourth, the record is stored in DynamoDB. Finally, the mobile app queries DynamoDB-backed order history and receives the saved order data. Now compare the three panels beneath the diagram. On the left, the original event contains event ID E V T one thousand one, order ID forty-two, an ORDER_PLACED event type, an amount of twenty-nine, and a timestamp. In the middle, Lambda has transformed that event into a record with order ID, status PLACED, amount, created-at and updated-at fields. On the right, those same fields appear as the DynamoDB item, with order ID as the partition key. So the event is not simply copied unchanged; it is converted into the format the application needs for querying. Finally, read the two panels at the bottom. Lambda can handle multiple Kinesis records per batch, but delivery or processing may be repeated after errors. That's why the slide calls out partial-failure handling and idempotency. A conditional write using order ID can help prevent duplicate records. The central lesson is that streaming captures what happened, Lambda shapes the data, and DynamoDB makes it available to the application.

scenes.title: Serverless web app request path
scenes.narration: This diagram zooms in on one request from a browser to a serverless backend and back again. Begin with the cyan arrows moving from left to right. In step one, the browser sends the HTTP request GET slash orders slash forty-two. API Gateway receives that request and, in step two, invokes a Lambda function. In step three, Lambda reads the order with ID forty-two from DynamoDB. Now follow the dashed orange arrows coming back toward the browser. DynamoDB returns the order item to Lambda in step four. Lambda produces the HTTP response in step five, and API Gateway returns it to the browser in step six. Notice that the arrows run in both directions: the request goes toward the database, and the response comes back to the user. The lower-left panel shows the actual request, including an Accept header for JSON. The lower-right panel shows a small JSON response: order ID forty-two, status shipped. This is what a mobile or web client can display as an order-status screen. The takeaway at the bottom divides responsibilities very clearly. API Gateway manages HTTP entry, Lambda runs the business logic, and DynamoDB stores the data. None of these services replaces the others. If a customer asks for an AI explanation of the status later, that model call belongs behind the same authorised application path, not directly inside the browser.

scenes.title: AWS Lambda — serverless compute
scenes.narration: Let's finish this first lecture by looking at what Lambda actually does. At the top, the diagram has three steps. An event from a service or application triggers a function. Lambda runs your code in response, without you managing the underlying servers. The function then returns a result or sends an output to another service. The icons on the left remind us that an event might come from S3, an API request, or another AWS service. Now move to the larger GenAI example at the bottom. Step one is validate request. Before calling a model, the function checks the input, applies business rules and prepares a prompt. Step two is invoke a model API: the function sends that prepared request to a foundation model and receives its generated output. Step three is transform response: the application parses the model's output, checks the expected format and prepares a useful result for the caller or downstream service. The panel on the right highlights three operational settings: execution duration, memory and concurrency. A function that runs too long, lacks enough memory or invokes too many model requests at once can fail even when its code is logically correct. Lambda gives us managed execution, but we still design the handler, permissions, limits and failure behavior. So remember the picture: an event starts the work, Lambda executes the logic, and the application uses the result.
